title: Remembering God's Deliverance - Habakkuk 3:16-19
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: Pastor Lyro examines Habakkuk 3:16-19 to show how remembering God's redemptive power—demonstrated supremely in the cross of Christ—enables believers to face life's difficulties with faith and rejoicing. The sermon explores how the love and terror of God's judgment are both revealed at the cross, transforming our perspective from fear to confidence in God's salvation.

outline.title: The Love of God Demonstrated in the Cross of Jesus Christ
subpoints: Habakkuk's emotional response (trembling lips, shaking knees) came from knowing God's redemptive power
The Exodus was the greatest display of God's redemptive power in the Old Testament
The cross of Christ is the ultimate and central redemptive event in salvation history
Nothing—neither tribulation, persecution, famine, nor any other circumstance—can separate us from God's love in Christ
God the Son stood condemned so that we could stand free

outline.title: The Terror of God Demonstrated in the Cross of Jesus Christ
subpoints: The cross reveals both God's love and God's judgment upon sin
The wrath of God was poured out upon Jesus Christ in our place
The cross displays the agony of sin and what God thinks of sin
The grotesque picture of the cross—the separation of the Son from the Father—shows the horror of sin's penalty
The wrath of God is appeased by the love of God at the cross

outline.title: Faith in God Demonstrated in a Change of Perspective
subpoints: Habakkuk's circumstances did not change, but his gaze shifted from the present to his Redeemer
Despite coming economic and military disaster, Habakkuk commits to rejoice in the Lord
The foundation of rejoicing is not circumstances but God Himself—the God of our salvation
Believers should count all earthly things as loss for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ
The Lord God alone is our strength; we are pilgrims looking toward the kingdom to come
Keeping our minds stayed on Jesus produces perfect peace

transcript:
## Reading of Habakkuk 3

> This is the Word of the Lord, the prayer of Habakkuk, the prophet.
>
> O Lord, I have heard your speech and was afraid. O Lord, revive your work in the midst of the years. In the midst of the years make it known; in wrath remember mercy. God came from Teman, the Holy One from Mount Paran. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of His praise. His brightness was like the light; He had rays flashing from His hand, and there His power was hidden. Before Him went pestilence, and fever followed at His feet. He stood and measured the earth; He looked and startled the nations. And the everlasting mountains were scattered; the perpetual hills bowed. His ways are everlasting. I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction; the curtains of the land of Midian trembled. O Lord, were You displeased with the rivers? Was Your anger against the rivers? Was Your wrath against the sea, that You rode on Your horses, Your chariots of salvation? Your bow was made quite ready; oaths were sworn over Your arrows. You divided the earth with rivers. The mountains saw You and trembled. The overflowing of the water passed by; the deep uttered its voice and lifted its hands on high. The sun and moon stood still in their habitation at the light of Your arrows they went, at the rushing of Your glittering spear. You marched through the land in indignation; You trampled the nations in anger. You went forth for the salvation of Your people, for salvation with Your anointed. You struck the head from the house of the wicked, laying bare from foundation to neck. You thrust through with his own arrows the head of his villages. They came out like a whirlwind to scatter me; their rejoicing was like feasting on the poor in secret. You walked through the sea with Your horses, through the heap of the great waters. When I heard, my body trembled; my lips quivered at the voice; rottenness entered my bones. My legs trembled beneath me, that I might rest in the day of trouble when he comes up to the people, he invades them with his troops. Though the fig tree may not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines; though the labor of the olive may fail, and the fields yield no food; though the flock may be cut off from the fold, and there be no herd in the stalls—yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The Lord God is my strength; He will make my feet like deer's feet, and He will make me walk on my high hills. (Habakkuk 3)

## Introduction

I notice this is not the first John. We are going through First John, but First John 5:6 and following present a particular challenge. There is a particular element in it that I want a little more wisdom before preaching on it. So I am saving it, Lord willing, for next week. This morning I want us to look at Habakkuk, and especially verses 16 through 19 of chapter 3. But it is important that we read the whole chapter so that those verses can be placed in context.

When you read Habakkuk, it is confusing. You don't get the warm fuzzies from reading it. It is no Isaiah 53. It is no Psalm 23. It is none of those more easily understood passages. But I think we can benefit from it as we consider it this morning.

## The Trembling of Habakkuk: Encountering God's Power

There are some events in life that cause your lips to quiver or your knees to knock. We see that in Habakkuk's experience in verse 16.

> I hear, and my body trembles. My lips quiver at the sound; rottenness enters into my bones. My legs tremble beneath me. Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us. (Habakkuk 3:16, ESV)

Habakkuk's lips are quivering. His legs are shaking. His knees are knocking because of what he heard from the Lord.

There are occasions in life where our lips quiver and our knees knock. Perhaps the birth of your first child. Or a teenage son saying, "I love you." Perhaps the sight of your bride coming down the aisle when you are officially waiting. I love looking at the groom as the bride is coming in, because there are so many emotions expressed on the face of the groom. Perhaps the testimony of what God has done in the life of a sister or a brother in Christ causes your lips to quiver. Or even perhaps a good sports movie—when the underdog player calls the fumble, recovers the ball, and scores a touchdown. Or perhaps a death in the family or a death in the church, or the news of tragedy, causes your lips to quiver and your knees to knock.

For Habakkuk, what made his lips quiver and his knees knock was knowing the power of God—knowing the power of God to deliver and the power of God to destroy.

## Three Things We See in Verses 16-19

I want for us to see three things as we look at these special verses:

1. The love of God demonstrated in the cross of Jesus Christ
2. The terror of God demonstrated in the cross of Jesus Christ
3. The faith in God demonstrated in a change of perspective

The first two points come from verse 16, and the last one comes from verses 17 through 19.

## The Love of God Demonstrated in the Cross of Jesus Christ

The book of Habakkuk is structured around questions that Habakkuk asked God. First, he was upset with the fact that the people of God in Israel—the church of his time—were not following the Lord. They were taking the Lord's name in vain in all they did. I don't mean just saying things, but they had the name of God upon them, yet they were acting as if God was not their God. They were squandering the blessings of the Lord.

Habakkuk cried before God and said, "God, how long are you going to let this go? Aren't you going to fix this? Aren't you going to punish or discipline your people? Aren't you going to rescue your name?"

God says, "Yes, Habakkuk, I'm going to do that. I'm going to do that by bringing the Chaldeans—that is, the Babylonians. More wicked people than Israel. They're going to come in and devastate you. And that's how I will judge my people."

Habakkuk hears that and goes, "Whoa, Lord. I didn't want you to act like that. I was thinking more like a gentle correction or something like that. But you're going to bring a more wicked nation to punish us? How's that going to work? How are people going to think about you? What are they going to think about you—that you're punishing your own people by a more wicked people?"

God says, "Habakkuk, the Just shall live by faith."

What He means by that is: Habakkuk, you are just. You are a righteous man. You have faith in Me. You believe that the Messiah is rising you. So live according to that faith. That faith tells you that I know what I'm doing. I will do what is right, whether you see it or not.

That's when we come to verse 16. When God answered Habakkuk's questions by saying that the Just will live by faith in God, Habakkuk turned his thoughts to the greatest display of God's redemptive power to date.

What do you think verses 3 through 15 are about? They talk about the rivers being divided. They talk about armies being drowned by the ocean. They talk about God having something against the rivers and the seas by splitting them. That's a reference to the Exodus. Not only the Exodus, but the conquering of the Promised Land.

In the mind of the Old Testament saint, the Exodus was the greatest display of God's redemptive power. God had delivered His people from the bondage of slavery in Egypt. God mercifully revealed Himself and gave them an identity by way of a covenant at Sinai. God purged them of their sins in the wilderness wanderings. God took them to a place of blessing that He had prepared for them in the Promised Land.

So the Exodus marked the beginning of God's constant, invisible presence with His people, and they treasured that. When an Old Testament saint wanted to know if God loved him, if an Old Testament saint wanted to know if God loved her, they would think about God's work of redemption in the Exodus. When they wanted to know if God was going to deliver them again, they would again look to God's work of redemption in the Exodus. They would look at Sinai and God's promise to be a God to them and to be a God to their children.

As Habakkuk remembered God's deliverance in verses 3 through 15—His redemption from slavery and redemption unto freedom and fellowship with God—his lips quivered. When we read about his deep emotion coming from within, it was based on the fact that he knew God as the Deliverer. His knees are knocking, his lips are quivering because of belief, driven by emotion—knowing God and what He had done for the old man. That's what's going on with Habakkuk here in verse 16.

For the saints in the Old Testament, when they wanted to know that God loved them, He had redeemed them from Egypt. God loved me. He placed me in the Promised Land. God loved me. Look at all the promises He made to us at Mount Sinai.

For us today, the cross is the major, ultimate, and glorious redemptive event in the history of God's people. The deliverance of God's people from Egypt was just a shadow pointing to the ultimate deliverance of God's people from His wrath and from sin in the cross of Jesus Christ. The cross is the focal, central, the most important event in the history of salvation. Beyond that, it is the greatest display, the greatest demonstration of God's love for His people.

So when you want to know that God loves you, what do you do? Do you look at the grandest demonstration of that love, the most objective, unquestionable demonstration of God's love for you—the cross of Jesus Christ? Is that where you look if you want to know that God loves you?

That's why we need to look, because it's objective. It cannot be questioned. In our honest life, life is often very challenging. To say it in more theological terms, life often stinks. Tragedy, heartbreak, disappointment can be part of living. And more often than not, they are part of living. Marriages fail. Kids rebel. Life is full of struggles. We face death, famine, old age, wars, wickedness all around. We look around and we are tempted to wonder if God really loves us.

But when we are tempted to do that, we need to take a hike up a little hill just outside of Jerusalem and see the cross of Christ on the hill of Calvary. Because on that hill, God crucified His Son because He loved us. There is nothing going on around us that can undo what God did for us on the cross of Calvary. He endured the cross for the joy set before Him—that is, His people.

Because of that, there is nothing that can separate us from the love of God in Jesus Christ. Do you believe that? We just recited that. We just affirmed that in our responsive reading of Romans 8.

> Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, or sword? No. In all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels, nor rulers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor anything else in all creation will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. (Romans 8:35, 37-39)

And you can add whatever you want to that list—it does not have the power to separate you from the love of God in Jesus Christ.

Why? Because of the cross of Jesus Christ. All of that—purchased, underserved sinners such as us. I think we often struggle with contentment and joy because I think I deserve something. I'm not even going to add the word "better" at the end. I just think I deserve something. And yet Scripture is talking about me as a worm—as one who is dead in trespasses and sins, as one who is going the opposite way. And yet God in His goodness and love rescued you through the cross of Calvary. And nothing can separate us from that Christ.

God the Son stood condemned so that we could stand free. We didn't read this part of Romans 8, but Paul says in verse 31 and following:

> What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also with Him graciously give us all things? (Romans 8:31-32)

All He requires of us is that we believe. He did that for us. And in talking to the Philippian jailer, Paul and Silas, when asked, "What do I need to do? What is it that I bring to the Lord? What do I need to do to get this salvation you're talking about?"—Paul and Silas told him, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household."

So in the cross of Christ, we have the love of God demonstrated.

## The Terror of God Demonstrated in the Cross of Jesus Christ

We also have the terror of God demonstrated in the cross of Christ.

> I hear, and my body trembles. My lips quiver at the sound; rottenness enters into my bones. My legs tremble beneath me. Yet I will quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon people who invade us. (Habakkuk 3:16)

The reality is that as Habakkuk thought about verses 3 through 15, he also saw the power of God in judgment. If God could destroy Egypt's army—the most powerful army in existence at the time—how much more will He do to this tiny nation in the hands of the Babylonians? That's what Habakkuk had to think about. This is the terror of God. That's the judgment of God upon the wicked. What is Babylon going to do with this tiny little nation that has no power? And they are coming with the most powerful army of the time. The weight of God's judgment made Habakkuk's knees knock.

We should have a similar reaction when we think of the cross, because the cross speaks not only of God's love, but also of God's judgment. When you look at the cross, you must see the terror of it. The Father judging sin on His Son. The terror of the wrath of God being poured upon Jesus. The separation of the Son from the Father—the cry, "My God, My God, why do You forsake Me?" The hell that the cross was. God Himself paying for the sins of His people—the Just for the unjust. A grotesque picture if we are going to be honest.

That's why Paul calls it the offense of the cross. That's why some have wrongly called it cosmic child abuse. It is a grotesque picture—the wrath of God poured upon His own Son. And when you look at the cross, you should see the awfulness of sin. The marred face of Jesus. The wounds. The nails. The crown of thorns. The bleeding back. That's all your sins doing.

We are talking about sin collectively getting Jesus to the cross. But if you had been the only person to ever live after Adam, you'd take the same cross to redeem just you. So you can very really say this: My sins got Him to the cross. Not just corporate sin, but my individual sins got Him to the cross. And the cross is a demonstration of what God thinks of sin. And Christ bore it with love.

John Newton says:

> I saw one hanging on the tree in agony and blood who fixed loving eyes on me as near His cross I stood. Never till my dying breath will I forget that look. It seemed to charge me with His death; they'll not aware of His spoke.

Every time you look at the cross, remember: you are charged with Jesus' death. But Newton continues:

> My conscience felt and owned the guilt and plunged me into despair. I saw my sin as blood had spilled and helped to nail Him there. But with a second look he said, "I freely offer you this blood as for your ransom paid. I died that you might live."

And then Newton concludes:

> Thus while His death my sin displays for all the world to see, such is the mystery of grace. It seals my pardon too with pleasing grief and mournful joy. My spirit now is filled that I should such a life destroy, yet live by Him I killed.

So we look at the cross and we see the wrath of God. But we see the wrath of God being appeased by the love of God. So the cross demonstrates the love of God, and the cross demonstrates the terror of God.

## Faith in God Demonstrated in a Change of Perspective

And as we embrace both of them in faith, then we're going to have a faith that's demonstrated in a change of perspective.

> Though the fig tree may not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines; though the labor of the olive may fail, and the fields yield no food; though the flock may be cut off from the fold, and there be no herd in the stalls—yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The Lord God is my strength; He will make my feet like deer's feet, and He will make me walk on His high hills. (Habakkuk 3:17-19)

Knowing that God is his Deliverer, Habakkuk is able to face this life with all its difficulties. Nothing has changed other than this: He gazed upon the Lord. That's the only change we have here from the rest of the book. He gazed upon the Lord.

Now with a much different attitude than he had in the beginning of the book, he comes before the Lord. He's not demanding answers anymore. He comes in trust. He says, "Even if all these bad things happen—the fig tree not blossoming, the vine not producing fruit, the olive not producing oil, and so on—if all this happens, I'm going to just trust in Him because 'the Just shall live by faith.'" (Habakkuk 2:4)

In verse 17, he describes the reason Habakkuk can quietly wait for the day of trouble to come upon the people who invade Israel as he says in verse 16. And Habakkuk's new commitment is to rejoice in the Lord.

Once he saw the beauty of God, he saw the love of God, the terror of God—he decides that he is going to rejoice in the Lord. It's a commitment he makes. We see that in verse 18:

> I will rejoice in the Lord. I will joy in the God of my salvation.

And notice that he is going to rejoice in God because of the God of his salvation. He understands that he doesn't need anything else if God is his salvation. It doesn't matter if the Babylonians are coming tomorrow to destroy him because God is the God of his salvation. It doesn't matter if everything is taken from him because God is the God of his salvation.

God is the God of your salvation. Use that to satisfy yourself with the God who saved you through Jesus Christ, who poured the guilt of your sins upon Him. Use that to satisfy yourself knowing that the love of God is never going to depart from you. Use that to satisfy yourself with knowing that there is nothing that can take your way or separate you from the love of God.

Habakkuk is now able to joy in the Lord. He is able to send out with the Apostle Paul:

> Whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as lost because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus as my Lord. For His sake I have suffered the loss of all things and count them as rubbish in order that I may gain Christ and be found in Him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ—the righteousness from God that depends on faith—that I may know Him and the power of His resurrection and may share His sufferings becoming like Him in His death. (Philippians 3:7-10)

In that sense, that's what Habakkuk exchanges in verse 18: "Yet I will rejoice in the Lord. I will joy in the God of my salvation."

Can you say that with the Apostle Paul? He's given you the grace. Christ is given you the grace to count everything—good things, bad things, sufferings—whatever it is as loss, that we may gain Christ. Do we want to gain Christ?

And because of that, Habakkuk's strength is renewed because now the Lord is his strength in verse 19:

> The Lord God is my strength.

Not the standing of Israel. Not his suffering. Nothing in this life is his strength. The Lord God is his strength. Yahweh, who delivered Israel from Egypt, is going to lift him up because he is not trusting on anything else. And he doesn't need anything else.

We are back at finally humbled himself. And the Scriptures say:

> Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, so that at the proper time He may exalt you. Cast all your anxieties on Him because He cares for you. (1 Peter 5:6-7)

## The Only Thing That Changed

Do you notice that nothing changed in Habakkuk's circumstances? Nothing, absolutely nothing. The Babylonians are still coming. They are still going to die, and it's going to be a death of suffering. They are going to be in captivity for 70 years, apart and away from the land that God has given them. That is all true. The only thing that changed was that he took his eyes off the here and now and placed it on his Redeemer. That's the only thing that changed in this whole passage.

What is Habakkuk trusting in? What is his gaze? Where is his gaze?

Are you ready to do that? Are you ready to take your eyes off the present—the here and now—and look to Christ who is coming again for you? Are you ready to not live life as permanent citizens of this place, but as pilgrims and sojourners of the life to come? Are you ready to see the beauty of your Savior face to face because you will be like Him when He comes back? And that's what drives you to live this life?

Are you living this life as if you were citizens of the future kingdom that were transported now and live a life that is so far into this world that people say, "Who is that weirdo?" Because we are citizens of the Jerusalem to come.

If you are ready for that, then think about Christ. Think about how ugly your sin is. Think about how He has dealt with it for you. And seek His kingdom and His righteousness.

The Lord says to the prophet Isaiah:

> You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on You because He trusts in You. (Isaiah 26:3)

What kind of peace? Perfect peace—the peace of whose mind is stayed on You.

This experience of keeping our minds upon Jesus is well expressed by the Puritan Samuel Rutherford in a letter to a parishioner who said, "Since He looked upon me"—talking about Christ—"Since Christ looked upon me, my heart's not my own. He that is Christ has run away to heaven with it."

Is your heart in heaven? Has Christ run away with your heart?
